role: Commander at the Battle of Mu'tah
Leader of the first Hijrah to Abyssinia
summary: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib (RA), known as al-Tayyar (the Flyer), was a cousin of the Prophet ﷺ, a leader of the first Hijrah to Abyssinia, and a commander who fell as a martyr at the Battle of Mu'tah. The Prophet ﷺ said he resembled him both in appearance and character, and that in Paradise he flies with two wings in place of his severed arms.
biography:
Ja'far ibn Abi Talib al-Hashimi al-Qurashi was born around 590 CE in Makkah to Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the uncle and protector of the Prophet ﷺ, making Ja'far a first cousin of the Prophet and an older brother of Ali ibn Abi Talib. He accepted Islam in the earliest years of the revelation, among the first wave of believers when the call was still secret. Ibn Sa'd records in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra that he accepted Islam before his brother Ali, at a time when few had yet declared their faith.

Around 615 CE, when persecution of Muslims in Makkah intensified, the Prophet ﷺ instructed a group of believers to emigrate to Abyssinia (al-Habasha) under the protection of its Christian king, the Negus (al-Najashi). Ja'far was chosen to lead this delegation, which numbered around eighty men and women in its second wave. When Quraysh sent emissaries — Amr ibn al-As and Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'ah — to convince the Negus to return the Muslims, Ja'far stood before the court and spoke on behalf of the group. He recited Surah Maryam before the Negus, who wept until his beard was wet and declared that the difference between what the Muslims described of Jesus and his own faith was no more than a line he drew on the ground. The emissaries of Quraysh returned empty-handed. This address is recorded in detail by Ibn Hisham in al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah and by Ibn Sa'd, and is considered one of the finest examples of early Muslim diplomacy.

Ja'far and his family remained in Abyssinia for approximately fifteen years, returning to Madinah in 7 AH (629 CE), the same year as the conquest of Khaybar. The Prophet ﷺ, upon seeing Ja'far return, embraced him and kissed him between the eyes, saying: 'I do not know what to be more delighted by — the conquest of Khaybar or the arrival of Ja'far.' (Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. 4)

Shortly after his return, Ja'far was appointed one of three commanders for the expedition to Mu'tah in 8 AH (629 CE), a village in what is now Jordan, where a Muslim force of three thousand faced a Byzantine-allied army reported in the sources as numbering over one hundred thousand. The Prophet ﷺ instructed that if the first commander, Zayd ibn Harithah, was killed, Ja'far should take command; and if Ja'far fell, then Abdullah ibn Rawahah. All three commanders were killed in the battle. Al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' and Ibn Kathir in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah record that Ja'far seized the standard after Zayd fell, fought fiercely on foot, and was struck with over ninety wounds to the front of his body — none to his back — before being killed. Both his hands were severed as he held the banner.

The Prophet ﷺ announced the news of the deaths to the Sahaba before messengers arrived, by divine disclosure (kashf). He wept for Ja'far and said: 'Ja'far has been given two wings in Paradise, and he flies with them wherever he wills.' This is why he is called al-Tayyar — the Flyer. The hadith is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim in the books on battles.

The Prophet ﷺ also said of Ja'far: 'You resemble me in appearance and character' — a statement considered among the highest distinctions given to any Sahabi. Al-Dhahabi notes that this resemblance was widely noted by those who knew both men. When Ja'far's family returned to Madinah after his martyrdom, the Prophet ﷺ visited his wife, Asma bint Umays, and wept with her over the three days she observed as the customary period of open grief.

Ja'far left behind three sons: Abdullah, Awn, and Muhammad — all born from his wife Asma bint Umays, who later married Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and then Ali ibn Abi Talib after Abu Bakr's death. He was martyred at approximately 39 years of age and is buried near the battlefield of Mu'tah in modern-day Jordan, where his tomb remains a site of visitation.

key_events.event: Accepted Islam in the earliest wave of believers
Led the second Hijrah to Abyssinia; delivered the famous address before the Negus
Returned to Madinah from Abyssinia on the day of the Khaybar conquest
Appointed commander at the Battle of Mu'tah; martyred after Zayd ibn Harithah fell

notable_traits: Exceptional eloquence and diplomatic skill — delivered the address to the Negus that preserved the Abyssinian sanctuary
Resembled the Prophet ﷺ in appearance and character by the Prophet's own testimony
Fierce courage at Mu'tah — no wounds to his back, over ninety to his front
Generous and charitable — nicknamed 'Abu al-Masakin' (Father of the Poor) for his care for the destitute
narrated_hadith_count: approximately 4 hadith in the major collections
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari — Kitab al-Maghazi (Battle of Mu'tah)
